entries.criterion: Lockstep is one tool, built to the single-tool design I approved and shipped from AES canonical: in a new repository one command sets it up, with one config file, in place of pcw, code2check and Company Planning's plan check.
demonstration: Open the Lockstep install walkthrough page (planned in slice 1, Q22)
Read the one command at the top (one line typed into a terminal in an empty repository) and the list of files it wrote
Open lockstep.yaml, the one settings file it wrote
Read the three hook entries it added: the small settings lines that make Claude Code, Codex and the commit checker (lefthook) call Lockstep automatically
entries.expected: In plain words: one typed command set everything up. It wrote lockstep.yaml and the three hook entries, installed from the agentic-engineering-system-canonical git address, and no second tool (pcw, code2check) had to be installed.
entries.failure_example: The walkthrough needs a second step such as installing code2check or copying a file by hand, or the command installs from the lockstep repository instead of AES canonical.
entries.status_note: Real run recorded in docs/planning/runs/lockstep-acceptance/a1.json (scripts/acceptance/a1.py); the run's own comparison says PASS on 2026-11-12. Brian has not judged it.

entries.criterion: When an agent tries to write a file the plan does not name, Lockstep refuses it and shows the plan; when it only reads a planned file, it is allowed.
demonstration: Open the guard replay page for lifelike (planned in slice 3)

Read the four rows. Each is an agent trying something: three ways of writing a new file that the plan does not list (cat >, echo >, python -c), and one that only copies a file for reading (read-only cp)
For each row, compare the column 'should' (what the plan says should happen) with the column 'did' (what the guard actually did)
Open the refused row's message
entries.expected: In plain words: an agent writing a file the plan does not list is refused; an agent only reading is allowed. The three writes show 'refused' in both columns and the refusal message lists the files the plan does allow; the read-only cp shows 'allowed' in both.
entries.failure_example: Today's Lockstep gets two of these wrong (DESIGN.md line 31): a 'did' column that says 'allowed' for cat > src/extra.py, or 'refused' for cp src/a.py /tmp/x, is a fail.
entries.status_note: Real run recorded in docs/planning/runs/lockstep-acceptance/a2.json (scripts/acceptance/a2.py); the run's own comparison says PASS on 2026-11-12. Brian has not judged it.

entries.criterion: A commit that breaks the plan's rules is refused at commit time: a new test that already passed before the change, an import the architecture diagram forbids, or a requirement with no Source line.
demonstration: Open the commit-check replay page (planned in slice 4)
Read one row per test commit: what it does, which check should refuse it, and what happened
Open the row for the test-first case and read the refusal message
entries.expected: Each of the three bad commits is refused by the named check (test-first, arch, sources) with a message naming the file or requirement; a clean commit in the same table is accepted.
entries.failure_example: The test-first row shows 'accepted' for a commit whose new test passes on the base revision, or the clean commit is refused.
entries.status_note: Real run recorded in docs/planning/runs/lockstep-acceptance/a3.json (scripts/acceptance/a3.py); the run's own comparison says PASS on 2026-11-12. Brian has not judged it.

entries.criterion: After a person approves the plan, the agent lays out the files, and each file's first docstring holds the normative text of what it must do, its success criteria and its tests, word for word from the approved plan.
demonstration: Open the layout page for a test repository (planned in slice 2)
Pick a planned file
Read the approved requirement and its scenarios on the left
Read the file's first docstring on the right
entries.expected: The docstring carries the requirement text, the success criteria and the test names exactly as approved; the page also shows that no file was laid out before the approval.
entries.failure_example: A docstring that paraphrases the requirement, leaves out the success criteria or test names, or a file that exists before the plan's approval date.
entries.status_note: Real run recorded in docs/planning/runs/lockstep-acceptance/a4.json (scripts/acceptance/a4.py); the run's own comparison says PASS on 2026-11-12. Brian has not judged it.

entries.criterion: The tool is configurable, portable and shareable: any repository, personal or Inside Success, installs it the same way; someone else can install it in their own repository from its public git address with only its README; a lockstep.yaml copied from one repository works in another; each check can be switched to block, warn or off; and nothing in it names my machine.
demonstration: Open the portability page (planned in slice 6)
Read the count of machine paths (folder names from Brian's own computer, such as /home/brian, written into the installed files) found in an installed repository
Read the table of checks and the setting each has in lockstep.yaml
Read the row for a repository outside BrianMills2718, installed by following the README only
Read the row where one repository's lockstep.yaml was copied into another
entries.expected: In plain words: the tool works on someone else's computer and repository without edits. The machine-path count is 0; every check has a block, warn or off setting; the owner and the human-source pattern come from lockstep.yaml, not from code; the outside repository installed from the README alone; the copied lockstep.yaml ran with only its owner line changed.
entries.failure_example: A path such as /home/brian or ~/code2 in an installed file, an owner hard-coded as BrianMills2718, a check that cannot be switched off, or an install that needs access to one of Brian's private repositories.
entries.status_note: Real run recorded in docs/planning/runs/lockstep-acceptance/a5.json (scripts/acceptance/a5.py); the run's own comparison says PASS on 2026-11-12. Brian has not judged it.

entries.criterion: A correction I gave an agent yesterday shows up today as a filed report in the feedback log, with my words.
demonstration: Open the agent-feedback-log issues filtered to source:human, newest first
Read the date of the newest issue
Open an issue from yesterday or today
Read the quote and the session it came from
entries.expected: The newest source:human issue is from the last night's run, and it quotes something you said in a session the day before.
entries.failure_example: No recent correction appears in the filed source:human issues, or a new nightly run again defers every correction behind other report types. The 867-report backlog observed on 2026-11-11 is historical: commit ec3022d5a records 867/867 filed, 0 errors.
entries.status_note: The page exists and the collector runs nightly. Q18 is resolved against the corrections-first repair and the 867/867 filing record in commit ec3022d5a; this reconciliation does not independently rerun the collector or judge today's issues.

entries.criterion: When I set a rule for agents, I can find it with my own words and the date, and see whether anything enforces it.
demonstration: Open code2-workspace agents/core.md on GitHub
Pick a rule that ends with your name and a date
Open agents/rule-sources.md and find the same rule
Read your words, the date and the incident behind it
entries.expected: Each rule in core.md names the date you said it, and rule-sources.md holds your words for it; the AES rules page says which list it covers.
entries.failure_example: A dated rule with no entry in rule-sources.md, or the AES rules page (docs/rules/RULES.md) claiming to list every rule agents follow while it lists one (today's state, Q20).
entries.status_note: The rule files exist; the AES register page's claim is open (Q20).

entries.criterion: I can see on one page what AES is: its three parts, where each lives, what runs today, and how far the one-tool build has got.
demonstration: Open the AES planning review page
Read the Architecture section's first view
Read the Plan and rollout section
entries.expected: Lockstep, the feedback loop and the policy layer are each named with the repository that holds them and what runs today (two feedback jobs on, three off); the plan section lists the six slices with which have merged.
entries.failure_example: The page still says AES is on hold, calls Lockstep retiring, or leaves out the feedback loop or the policy layer.
entries.status_note: Built by this package refresh; Brian has not judged it.

entries.criterion: A source-owned plan status, description, interface or evidence value updates its declared wiki copy after an edit, and a stale copy is refused when refresh is bypassed.
demonstration: Open the linked source-fact acceptance table, then its Company Planning reader page.
For each of the four fact types, compare the source change, expected copied value and recorded result.
Read the installed hook replay and native-client dispatch rows separately.
Read the bypass row: a source-only change must fail the read-only project check without that check rewriting the page.
entries.expected: All four fact types copy the source value; the installed refresh command updates the declared block; a bypassed refresh is refused by the read-only merge check. Native dispatch is claimed only after a fresh Claude Code or Codex session records the callback.
entries.failure_example: Plan 61 says done while its declared wiki block says active and the project check still passes; or a successful command replay is presented as proof that a native client dispatched the hook.
entries.status_note: Provider merged in AES #844; paired reader delivered in Company Planning #301, with 11/11 command cases, 2/2 native fixtures, canonical Codex admission and exact served-revision evidence. Not yet judged by Brian.
